evidence_quotes.quote: Additionally, users were asked with which actors in the water institutional arena they had experienced conflict over water in the past two years and whether the conflict was over water for irrigation or for domestic use.

This type of conflict includes all disputes over water for domestic use identified in this study and involves the three types of actors in the institutional arena who are charged with water management for domestic use: the OOMAPAS; a water purifier; tankers; an Ejido commissioner (who is also an institutional actor influencing water management); and 14 users.

Users say that this central water conflict is due to OOMAPAS’ poor service and high fees. The communities have organized to seek alternatives involving self-management, of which two modalities were identified: community wells and artisanal wells.

Although Mexico reformed its Constitution in 2012 to include the human right to water, Mexico has yet to modify its National Water Law and the corresponding regulations (Ávila-García 2016; Wilder et al. 2020).

This study is based upon the following central question: what are the types of conflict between users and actors that influence the water management of an irrigation district in northwest Mexico? Based on social network analysis, conflicts were conceptualized as a type of negative link, and a community detection algorithm was applied to identify the types of conflicts. This information was triangulated with ethnographic fieldwork.

criterion_notes.c1: Primarily studies agricultural irrigation water and farmland rental conflicts in the Rio Mayo Irrigation District (RMID) (Subgroups 1 and 2), which are outside household/community water service scope; however, the survey explicitly differentiated conflicts over irrigation water vs. domestic water, and Subgroup 3 (n = 14 users, Section 4.2.3) empirically examines household and community domestic water supply involving the local potable water and sanitation utility (OOMAPAS), community-managed wells, household artisanal wells, purified drinking water, and tankers.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 but FAILS the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Plain wording: YES — Subgroup 3 examines institutional and governance factors in domestic water provision, specifically conflictive ties between indigenous/female ejido users and domestic water institutions (municipal utility OOMAPAS, Ejido commissioner, tankers, water purifiers) and community self-governance via local well committees ('vernacular systems of water management'). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — all specific legal, tenure, and administrative rules discussed in the paper (1992 Constitutional Article 27/PROCEDE ejido land reform, 1992 National Water Law concessions, irrigation module water-programming rules, and canal-worker gatekeeping discretion) govern agricultural irrigation water and farmland rental, not household/community drinking-water or sanitation access. Conversely, for domestic water (Subgroup 3), the study does not empirically analyze any rule-type mechanism governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation requirements for domestic connections, specific tariff or cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or regulatory structure); it merely clusters negative social-network conflict ties attributed generally to OOMAPAS 'poor service and high fees', describes informal community/artisanal well self-supply, and cites secondary literature on Mexico's 2012 constitutional right to water and unamended National Water Law as unanalysed macro-governance background.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary mixed-methods empirical evidence collected between March 2021 and August 2022: 6 open interviews with key institutional actors, 118 structured interviews with RMID users analyzed via bimodal social network analysis and the Girvan-Newman community detection algorithm, and ethnographic fieldwork.
criterion_notes.c4: Although the quantitative SNA outcome is membership in water-conflict clusters ('negative links' over the prior two years) rather than a quantitative service-access metric, the qualitative ethnographic component for Subgroup 3 (Section 4.2.3) reports household and community domestic water access outcomes, including non-delivery of piped water despite holding an OOMAPAS domestic contract, refusal to supply piped water from the municipal seat, perceived high fees, well-water salinity degradation, and reliance on community wells, artisanal wells, purified water, and emergency tankers.
criterion_notes.c5: Provides sufficient information to identify the population and sample (118 RMID landholder users in Sonora, Mexico, including 14 users in domestic-water Subgroup 3; dyadic user-actor conflict ties), broad sociodemographic and institutional exposures, conflict-cluster and qualitative domestic-supply outcomes, and a cross-sectional ('transversal') mixed-methods SNA and ethnographic study design (though lacking an empirical rule-type domestic water governance exposure per Criterion 2).
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

study_design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods study combining bimodal social network analysis (Girvan-Newman community detection on 118 structured user interviews) with 6 open key-informant interviews and ethnographic fieldwork
population_and_sample: Users (agricultural plot landholders with ejido or private property tenure) of the Rio Mayo Irrigation District (RMID) in Sonora, Mexico (N = 118 surveyed users out of 11,452 RMID users, of whom 49 reported water conflicts including n = 14 in the domestic-water subgroup; plus 6 open interviews with key institutional actors and ethnographic fieldwork; unit of analysis: individual RMID user and user-actor conflict dyad)
exposure: User sociodemographic and agrarian attributes (gender, education, age, indigenous ethnicity and language, ejido vs. private agricultural land tenure, farming vs. renting out plots, leadership positions) and institutional water-management arena interactions (irrigation modules, canal workers, large-scale farmers, and in Subgroup 3 domestic water actors: municipal utility OOMAPAS, water purifiers, tankers, and Ejido commissioner vs. vernacular community/artisanal well self-management)
outcome: Self-reported water-conflict ties over the past two years conceptualized as negative links in a bimodal social network and partitioned into four subgroups via Girvan-Newman community detection (agricultural irrigation and land-rental conflicts in Subgroups 1-2; domestic water conflicts in Subgroup 3 accompanied by qualitative accounts of OOMAPAS non-delivery despite contract, lack of municipal piped supply, perceived high fees, well-water salinity, and reliance on community wells, artisanal wells, purified water, and tankers)
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification of Criterion 2. Most of the study examines agricultural irrigation water and farmland rental conflicts among landholders in the Rio Mayo Irrigation District (Subgroups 1 and 2), where legal and institutional rules (1992 agrarian/ejido land reform, 1992 National Water Law concessions, irrigation module water programming, and canal-worker gatekeeping) govern agricultural crop irrigation rather than household or community service access. Although Subgroup 3 (n = 14 users) touches on household and community domestic water supply (conflicts with municipal utility OOMAPAS, tankers, and water purifiers vs. vernacular community and artisanal wells), the domestic-water component analyzes only social-network conflict ties ('negative links'), generic complaints of 'poor service and high fees', community self-supply workarounds, and unanalysed macro-governance background on Mexico's unamended National Water Law—not any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing domestic water or sanitation service access. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, Subgroup 3's institutional governance comparison and qualitative domestic access accounts would qualify for inclusion.
